newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Outlook bleak for Czech building stocks - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Outlook bleak for Czech building stocks - analysts.

text.p: A weak economy, cuts in public spending and soaring interest rates mean Czech construction industry offers few opportunities for equity investors and existing shareholders should hold or sell their stakes, analysts polled by Reuters said on Wednesday.

In the first four months of 1997, real construction output fell by 1.7 percent and shares in the four building companies listed on the Prague bourse's PX50 index fell on average by 27 percent, underperforming a falling index by around 22 percent.
"Basically at the moment its pretty awful," said ING Baring's Anna Bossong.
"Prospects are not particularly good. The industry has been talking about margin cuts now for a steady six months. So I've just put my recommendations to hold or sell," she said.
The four construction stocks quoted on the PX50 are IPS Praha a.s., Metrostav a.s., Vodni Stavby Praha a.s. and Stavby Silnic a Zeleznic a.s..
Taken together they account for 2.2 percent of the PX50's capitalisation.
On Wednesday, Vodni Stavby was the only gainer on the index, rising 45 crowns to 955, IPS fell six to 725 and the others were unchanged.
The crisis in the cyclical building industry forms part of a broader downturn in the Czech economy.
The government has said that figures which will be released by the statistical office on Thursday will probably show no gross domestic product growth in the first quarter.

In response to the problems, which threaten to push the state budget into the red, the government has inaugurated an austerity programme featuring hefty cuts in public expenditure and a public sector pay freeze.
"State orders for construction are going to dry up because of the budget cuts," warned Lindsay Ashford, a construction industry analyst at Zivnostenska Banka.

Just as importantly for construction companies, which often turn to banks for short term borrowing, interest rates have risen to extraordinary levels in the wake of the crisis surrounding the Czech crown.

Overnight interbank rates were quoted at 35 percent on Wednesday but exceeded 150 percent at the height of the crown crisis. After the central bank floated the currency it raised the discount rate to 13 percent from 10.5.

"Companies with high debt/equity ratios will suffer at the moment... many construction companies will be in trouble in the next few months if interest rate are not going down rapidly," said Miroslav Nosal of Patria Finance, pointing out that many of the companies are highly geared.

The only faint glimmer of hope for investors was that eventually public infrastructure projects would have to be completed offering potentially high returns to the larger companies and their suppliers.
Nosal added that big companies could also benefit as smaller companies folded under the weight of the industry crisis thus eliminating competition.
"It can easily happen that stronger companies will become even stronger while small comanies will fail," he said. ---------------------------------------------------------
